title: Null safety — quick overview
rememberThis: `int?` is `System.Nullable<int>` at run time — a struct with HasValue. `string?` is still `System.String`; the `?` is a compiler annotation only.
Nullable reference type (NRT) warnings are not NullReferenceExceptions. A warning-clean build can still throw at run time from JSON, Redis, or missing message attributes.
Prefer `ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull` and real checks over `!`. Treat `!` as a compiler lie you must prove at run time.
`required` forces initialization in an object initializer — it does not forbid null. Combine `required` with a non-nullable type when null is invalid.
TypeScript strictNullChecks and C# NRT both disappear at run time on references. Only `Nullable<T>` is a real CLR type for value types.
bullets: Enable `<Nullable>enable</Nullable>` in the project file (modern templates already do). Use `#nullable` pragmas for legacy file islands.
Flow analysis tracks not-null vs maybe-null. `if (x is not null)` narrows null-state for the rest of the block.
Auth tokens, Redis cache misses, and CSV empty cells are the usual maybe-null surfaces — annotate them with `?`, do not bang them with `!`.
Analysis attributes (`NotNullWhen`, `MaybeNull`, `NotNullIfNotNull`) teach the compiler contracts it cannot infer from signatures alone.
Lifted operators on `int?` return null when any operand is null. Relational comparisons with null yield false — a common interview trap.

rows.label: int?
rows.value: Nullable<int> struct; HasValue / Value; boxing a null int? boxes to a null reference

rows.label: string?
rows.value: Same Intermediate Language (IL) type as string; compiler warns on assign/dereference mismatch

rows.label: x!
rows.value: Suppresses warnings only; evaluates as x at run time — no guard

rows.label: ThrowIfNull
rows.value: Runtime guard that throws; also updates null-state after the call via NotNull attribute

rows.label: required
rows.value: C# 11+: must be set in an object initializer; can still be set to null if the type allows it
